stories.headline: US slaps 50% tariffs on $20 billion of Canadian goods after talks blow up
stories.dek: Duties hit about 5% of what Canada sells to America. Ottawa says it will hit back on Sept. 8.
stories.caveman: America and Canada used to be best shop friends. That fight got worse this weekend. After talks in Washington died late Friday, the US put a 50 percent tax on about 20 billion dollars of Canadian stuff, starting Saturday. That is about 5 percent of what Canada sells south. Hockey sticks, cement, tongue depressors. Trump used an old 1930 law, Section 338, that nobody had used for tariffs before. Canada Prime Minister Mark Carney said America asked too much and offered too little, then sent his team home. He said Canada will hit back dollar for dollar starting Sept. 8, on steel, dairy, farm machines, paper, and electronics. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said America was answering Canadian hits. Big US bosses at the Business Roundtable warned prices will rise for American families. Border-state governors yelled too. No new talks are booked.
stories.why_it_matters: A tax war with your biggest neighbor makes cars, food, and lumber cost more on both sides. It also poisons the North America trade pact both still need to rewrite.
stories.camps: Trump camp says Canada free-rides and must pay. Carney says last-minute US terms were unfair and even poked Quebec language. US companies want talks back. Shoppers will see the bill first.

terms.explain: A tax on stuff coming in from another country.
A 1930 US law that lets the president tax a country up to 50% if he says it treats American business unfair. Never used for tariffs before this fight.
The trade pact of the US, Mexico, and Canada. Trump will not keep it as it is.

stories.image_alt: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney speaking about US tariffs in Ottawa
stories.image_credit: Photo: Patrick Doyle / The Canadian Press via AP

stories.headline: Stocks bounce Friday, still lose the week as long US yields stay high
stories.dek: Dow up about 1% Friday. S&P 500 and Nasdaq up about 0.4%. All three still finished the week down.
stories.caveman: Wall Street got a small hug Friday and still went home sad for the week. The Dow rose about 1 percent. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq rose about 0.4 percent. For the whole week the S&P 500 fell about 1.4 percent, the Nasdaq about 2.1 percent, the Dow about 0.8 percent. The 10-year US yield sat near 4.73 percent. The 30-year sat near 5.27 percent. High yields make future tech profits look smaller, so growth stocks got punched. Oil stayed expensive: Brent around 94 dollars, US crude around 87. Gold held near 4,675 dollars. Next week watchers stare at Wednesday: the Fed's favorite inflation print, and Nvidia's earnings after the bell. Jackson Hole, the Wyoming money camp, is still a week away.
stories.why_it_matters: If long-term yields stay this high, mortgages, car loans, and company borrowing stay dear. A one-day bounce does not wipe a week of rate fear plus war oil.
stories.camps: Bulls say Friday's rebound and still-growing US services show the economy is not dead. Bears say oil plus fat yields will keep squeezing stocks, especially chips, until someone blinks.

terms.explain: The interest a bond pays. When yields jump, new borrowing gets pricier.
A US government measure of what people pay. The Fed watches it closer than the regular CPI sticker.
A yearly Fed camp in Wyoming. This year's is Aug. 27 to 29. New Chair Kevin Warsh speaks Friday Aug. 28.

stories.image_alt: Traders on the New York Stock Exchange floor

stories.headline: Four in five Hormuz tankers go dark so Gulf oil can still sneak out
stories.dek: Kpler: about 80% of Hormuz traffic turned off trackers in two weeks. US Energy says 8 to 9 million barrels a day still move.
stories.caveman: The skinny sea door by Iran is still a war zone. So oil boats are playing ghost. Shipping data shop Kpler says about 80 percent of Hormuz trips in the last two weeks switched off their tracker beacons and hugged the Oman side, as far from Iran as they can. The US Navy helps guard that south path. US Energy says 8 to 9 million barrels a day still go through, about twice what some Wall Street trackers see, because those trackers only count boats that stay visible. Before the war it was about 15 million. Saudi Arabia also pipes about 5 million barrels a day west to the Red Sea. The trick is buying time. War has already eaten as much as 1.9 billion barrels from storage. At least 15 boats on the south path have been hit since June. Brent still sits in the mid-90s, not 120, because this ghost fleet plus extra oil from Brazil, Guyana, Venezuela, and the US is plugging the hole. For now.
stories.why_it_matters: If the ghost trick fails, pump prices jump again and inflation comes back as the Fed's uninvited guest. Taiwan pays it in shipping and in the cost of stuff on boats.
stories.camps: Washington says dark runs plus escorts keep the world fed with oil. Iran says the squeeze is economic war and the strait is still a weapon. Traders price a long mess, not a total shut door.

terms.explain: A skinny sea door by Iran. In peacetime a lot of the world's oil boats go through it.
The radio box on a ship that tells the world where it is. Turning it off makes the ship hard to see on public maps.
Ships that hide their trackers. Iran used this to sell oil under sanctions. Now Gulf oil uses a version of it to dodge attacks.

stories.image_alt: Oil tanker at sea near the Gulf

stories.headline: Nvidia reports Wednesday as oil, yields, and Iran keep the tape jumpy
stories.dek: The chip giant reports after the bell Aug. 26, same morning as the Fed's favorite inflation print.
stories.caveman: Next big money test is Wednesday. Nvidia, the US chip shop that sells the brains for most AI, tells Wall Street how the quarter went after the closing bell. That same morning Washington prints PCE, the inflation number the Fed likes most. The week just ended already hurt tech: the Nasdaq dropped about 2 percent. High 30-year yields near 5.27 percent make far-off AI profits look cheaper. War oil near 94 dollars makes inflation harder to kill. New Fed Chair Kevin Warsh does not speak at Jackson Hole until next Friday, so Wednesday's two prints will do a lot of talking first. If Nvidia's future sales look soft, or if inflation stays sticky, the market can gap down before anyone even flies to Wyoming.
stories.why_it_matters: Nvidia is the thermometer for the whole AI spend. A miss plus a hot inflation print would tell bosses: money stays expensive, and war oil is still in the machine.
stories.camps: Bulls say companies still cannot buy enough chips. Bears say the easy AI trade already ran, and yields plus oil will clip it. Warsh has been quiet on rates. Markets hate quiet.

terms.explain: US company that makes the chips most AI computers use.
The inflation gauge the Fed prefers. Out Wednesday with income and spending numbers.
New US central bank boss since May 2026. First Jackson Hole speech is Aug. 28.

stories.image_alt: Nvidia headquarters or chip visual

stories.headline: A nameless coding model called Ox Alpha floods OpenRouter and nobody owns it
stories.dek: Free preview since Thursday. Stripe boss Patrick Collison called it very impressive. Fingerprints point at China's Z.ai. Nobody confesses.
stories.caveman: A new robot brain for writing code showed up Thursday on OpenRouter, a US shop that lets you rent many AIs from one door. The listing name is Ox Alpha. No company name. No press note. It is free for a short look. It says it can hold about a million words of context, see pictures and video, and keep working as an agent. Stripe chief Patrick Collison, whose firm is buying OpenRouter, posted that it is very impressive. By Sunday, code forums were doing detective work. Some error messages and word-piece tests match GLM models from Chinese lab Z.ai, also called Zhipu. Other people guessed Microsoft. OpenRouter only says a third party asked to stay secret. The catch: the stealth-model rules let the hidden owner keep your prompts to train on. You cannot name who is holding the diary.
stories.why_it_matters: If a frontier coding brain can hide its maker, shops cannot check safety, spies, or where your code goes. Cheap and nameless is a feature for users and a fog for everyone else.
stories.camps: Fans say try the tool, the name can wait. Safety people say a free mystery model that keeps every prompt is a gift to whoever sits behind the curtain. China hawks want a flag on the listing. Z.ai has not claimed it.

terms.explain: A US marketplace that lets developers call many AI models through one door. Stripe is buying it.
An AI listed with no company name while the maker tests it in public.
A Chinese AI lab. Online tests say Ox Alpha's fingerprints look like its GLM family. The lab has not said it is theirs.

stories.image_alt: Developer using a coding AI interface

stories.headline: US AI labs still will not publish a plan to cage a model that goes rogue
stories.dek: Guidelight graded five labs Saturday. OpenAI scored highest on containment. Anthropic and Meta scored zero on that one box.
stories.caveman: A US safety shop called Guidelight AI Standards looked at public papers from OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, xAI, and Meta. Question: if your robot starts ducking human control, what exact steps do you take, and when do you pull the plug? Almost nobody answers in writing. OpenAI scored best, 3 out of 5, because it has paused inside jobs after safety messes and said what it would do before turning them back on. It still has no full pre-set plan. Anthropic, the lab that sells itself as the careful one, scored zero on publishing a containment plan. Meta also scored zero. Google wrote the most detailed future map but has not built most of it yet. Guidelight only grades what is public, so a secret inside plan would not count. California already makes big labs publish how they handle ugly incidents. New York's similar law starts in January. A US bill would force a kill switch.
stories.why_it_matters: These models now sit inside company computers and can take actions, not just chat. If a lab is winging the emergency, the rest of us live with that bet.
stories.camps: Labs say the report misses private work and that spelling out a kill plan can create legal risk. Guidelight says if you cannot show the plan, assume you do not have one. Safety hawks want the kill-switch bill.

terms.explain: A pre-set plan to cut a model's powers or shut it off if it tries to dodge human control.
A US group that grades big AI labs on public safety practices. Its scientist Steven Adler used to work at OpenAI.
AI that does multi-step jobs on its own inside a computer, not just answers a chat.

stories.image_alt: Abstract AI safety or server visual

stories.headline: Dutch privacy cops fine Uber about 1 billion dollars for robot-firing drivers
stories.dek: 825 million euros. Second-biggest GDPR hit ever. Uber will appeal.
stories.caveman: The Dutch privacy office, which watches Uber's Europe HQ, said Friday the ride app used computers alone to freeze or kill driver accounts from 2018 to 2022. EU law says you cannot let a machine make a life-changing call with no human in the loop. The office also said Uber did not tell drivers clearly that a robot was judging them. Fine: 825 million euros, about 966 million dollars, a slice of Uber's 2025 sales of about 44.5 billion euros. Only Meta's 1.2 billion euro data-transfer fine is bigger under this law. Uber says the number is wild, that fraud pauses were short, that it never let a computer permanently fire people, and that only 126 Europe drivers lost accounts for low ratings in 2021. It will appeal. This is the Dutch office's fourth Uber fine.
stories.why_it_matters: A robot that can take your paycheck with no human check is the gig-work nightmare. A billion-dollar slap says Europe will still bill US platforms for it years later.
stories.camps: The Dutch office says automated firing without a person is illegal, period. Uber says humans now review, drivers can appeal, and the old cases were few. Drivers' groups say the fine is late but the fear was always real.

terms.explain: Europe's big personal-data law. It bans fully automated decisions that hit people hard, unless strict rules are met.
A computer decides your fate with no human looking first.
The Netherlands data watchdog. It polices Uber in Europe because Uber's EU base is there.

stories.image_alt: Uber sign at company headquarters

stories.headline: Flock's camera boss begs for a 'compromise' as America turns on plate spies
stories.dek: Sunday TechCrunch: CEO Garrett Langley did a Fox tour. Police allegedly used the network to stalk partners. Default data keep-time fell from 30 days to 7.
stories.caveman: Flock Safety is the US company that plasters neighborhoods with cameras that read license plates. CEO Garrett Langley spent the weekend on TV saying the country must pick both privacy and safety, not one. The Washington Post logged 46 cases of cops accused of using Flock to follow wives, girlfriends, or exes. Langley told CBS he was sorry it happened, then said Flock did not invent cop abuse, it just made the abuse visible. Default keep-time dropped from 30 days to 7. Searches now need a case code. Both rules can be turned off. The ACLU says 7 days is still longer than the 48 hours it wants. Bernie Sanders told people to stop Flock. Three House Republicans filed a bill to block federal money for this kind of camera. Some towns are ripping the units down. Langley wants states to make illegal lookups a crime, not just a firing.
stories.why_it_matters: A private company now runs a coast-to-coast car diary for police. If the diary is easy to peek at, stalking is not a glitch. It is the product.
stories.camps: Flock says the cameras solve crimes and find missing people, and that new audits will catch dirty cops. Privacy groups say a compromise that still lets police override the lock is not a lock. Left and right both smell a panopticon.

terms.explain: US firm that sells automatic license-plate cameras, and now drones, to police and HOAs.
A camera that reads car plates and stores when and where the car passed.
Flock setting that lets police keep plate data longer than the new 7-day default.

stories.image_alt: Automatic license plate reader camera on a US street pole
stories.image_credit: Photo: Smith Collection / Gado / Getty Images / TechCrunch

stories.headline: Zelensky says Russia will likely draft 300,000 more men after next month's vote
stories.dek: Sunday remarks. He says Putin told generals to finish taking Donetsk this year. Kyiv also wants more US Patriot missiles.
stories.caveman: Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky said Sunday Russia will probably call up at least 300,000 more soldiers after parliamentary elections next month. He thinks the new men will be thrown at Donetsk, the east region Moscow still does not fully own. Zelensky claimed Russia has already lost about 267,000 troops this year, about 155,000 of them dead. Those numbers cannot be checked from outside. He said Ukraine still holds about 20 percent of Donetsk, including the factory cities Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, and that Russia cannot finish the job. He also said US Patriot missiles are drying up: 675 in 2023, a forecast of only 264 this year. He asked Washington to sell even 10 percent of its Patriot stock, paid for by Kyiv. Talks with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, he said, are stuck because Russia still wants Ukraine to walk away from Donbas.
stories.why_it_matters: A fresh 300,000-man wave would mean another winter of meat-grinder war, more refugees, and more pressure on a thin US air-defense cupboard.
stories.camps: Zelensky says Russia will burn the new draftees in Donetsk and still fail. Moscow has not confirmed a draft and hates talking about losses. Trump's envoys want a deal that does not look like a Ukrainian surrender. Patriots are the only tool that reliably kills ballistic missiles.

terms.explain: When a state orders civilians into the army. Russia's 2022 draft sent many young men abroad.
An eastern Ukraine region Russia wants to swallow whole. Kyiv still holds a belt of cities there.
US air-defense missiles. They are the main tool Ukraine has to shoot down Russian ballistic missiles.

stories.image_alt: Volodymyr Zelensky speaking about the war

stories.headline: Ukrainian drones hit two Russian fighter jets, an S-400 nest, and a string of radars
stories.dek: Unmanned Systems Forces say 11 of 14 targets were hit Sunday across Rostov, Krasnodar, and occupied Crimea.
stories.caveman: Ukraine's drone army said Sunday it smashed a long list of Russian eyes and teeth. Commander Robert Brovdi, call sign Magyar, said crews hit 11 of 14 targets. In Vityazevo, on the Krasnodar coast about 300 kilometers from the front, they say they struck a Su-33 fighter, a MiG-29 fighter, and an Orion spy drone. They also claim an S-400 battery near Gelendzhik, a Pantsir in Yeysk, a Tor launcher, and eight radars from occupied Crimea to Rostov. Zelensky said Saturday a Su-24 bomber and four other air pieces were wrecked at Saky airfield in Crimea. Russia did not confirm the jet kills. The point is not one airfield. It is a months-long hunt for the radars that tell Russian missiles where to fly and tell Russian jets when to hide.
stories.why_it_matters: If Ukraine can keep blinding radars deep inside Russia, it makes room for its own strikes and makes Russia's expensive air-defense net look leaky.
stories.camps: Kyiv releases cockpit video and target lists. Moscow stays quiet or calls it propaganda. Independent plane-spotters try to match wreckage. The campaign is real even when each tail number is not.

terms.explain: Russia's long-range air-defense system. Meant to kill jets and missiles far away.
Ukraine's dedicated drone branch. Its commander uses the call sign Magyar.
Short-range Russian anti-air guns and missiles used to protect bigger systems like the S-400.

stories.image_alt: Ukrainian drone or damaged Russian air-defense site
stories.image_credit: Photo: Unmanned Systems Forces / Kyiv Post

stories.headline: Trump says Canada wants to be a US state without the paperwork
stories.dek: Sunday Truth Social blast after Carney called the new tariffs an attack and killed the talks.
stories.caveman: After the 50 percent tariffs landed Saturday, Canada Prime Minister Mark Carney called it an attack. 'You are at war when you get attacked,' he said. Ontario Premier Doug Ford said Trump is the kind of man who steals your lunch money. On Sunday Trump posted that Canada wants the benefits of being a US state without being one, and that Canada has taxed American farmers for years. He has floated swallowing Canada as the 51st state before. Canadians hate it. A petition to kick out US Ambassador Pete Hoekstra has about 248,000 names. Carney, a former central banker elected to stand up to Trump, froze talks and sent negotiators back to Ottawa. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said no new talks are planned. Democrats from border states say this is a price spike dressed up as patriotism.
stories.why_it_matters: When the White House talks about Canada as a wannabe state, this is no longer just a tax fight. It is a trust break between two countries that share an unguarded border.
stories.camps: Trump says Canada free-rides. Carney says America changed and writes its name in pencil. Ford wants every tool used. US border governors want the grown-ups back in the room.

terms.explain: Canada's prime minister. He used to run the central banks of Canada and Britain. He won office promising to push back on Trump.
Trump's gag and threat that Canada should become another US state. Most Canadians treat it as an insult.
Trump's top trade bargainer. He says America is done talking for now.

stories.image_alt: Donald Trump speaking, with Canada-US trade tension in the news

stories.headline: Iran's security chief: not one drop of Gulf oil if the US squeeze goes on
stories.dek: Iran's security chief, per IRNA. Central bank already says Iranian oil sales are at zero. Bessent still tees up 'toughest sanctions in history.'
stories.caveman: Iran's top security official Rezaei said Tehran will not let a single drop of oil leave the Gulf or Hormuz if Washington keeps piling on economic war. He also threatened other export paths. The line ran on state media. Iran's central bank chief already said last week that oil exports have in practice fallen to zero, and that friends abroad told him the money is gone. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is still lining up what he calls the toughest sanctions in history, aimed in part at China, which buys most of the Iranian barrels that still move. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman was in France Sunday to talk with President Macron about other sea and pipe routes. Iran's parliament also floated fees on boats using Hormuz. Independent reporters have not confirmed those fees are real in the water. The June 17 pause deal is dead. Both capitals talk like this can last months.
stories.why_it_matters: If Iran tries to bottle the whole Gulf, not just its own barrels, every pump on earth moves. Even a threat that large is a tax on food, freight, and rate cuts.
stories.camps: Tehran says the squeeze is economic terrorism and the strait is leverage. Washington says collapse the regime without going back to big ground war. Beijing tells both sides to talk. Gulf states hunt backup pipes.

terms.explain: Iran's top security official. He spoke through state media about blocking Gulf oil.
US Treasury boss. He has promised the toughest Iran sanctions yet and says America probably will not restart large combat.
A June US-Iran paper that briefly eased the fight and let talks run 60 days. Both sides now treat it as finished.

stories.image_alt: Strait of Hormuz or Iranian official related to the oil standoff

stories.headline: Ann Patchett's Whistler holds No. 2 as US indie shops keep selling quiet grief
stories.dek: IndieBound list for the week ending Aug. 19, posted through the weekend. 11 weeks on the hardcover fiction chart.
stories.caveman: Ann Patchett is the US novelist who also owns Parnassus Books in Nashville. Her new novel Whistler sits at No. 2 on the national indie hardcover fiction list for the week ending Aug. 19. It has been there 11 weeks. The book follows Daphne Fuller, 53, who meets her old stepfather Eddie again in a New York museum. Their short family tie ended in a hard event when she was nine. Now they refuse to lose each other a second time. Indie Next picked it No. 1 for June. The No. 1 slot is still Yesteryear, the tradwife-in-1855 debut we will not re-litigate. Under Patchett, shoppers are choosing a short, adult novel about memory and care, not another dungeon crawl. Patchett has a Pulitzer-finalist book, a National Humanities Medal, and a bookstore. When her name sits at No. 2 this long, independents are telling you what they can still hand-sell.
stories.why_it_matters: Indie lists are a weather report for US literary fiction. Patchett holding No. 2 means readers still pay 30 dollars for a small human story in a loud summer.
stories.camps: Patchett fans call Whistler her late-style tender book. Some critics want more plot. Booksellers like that it is short enough to finish and rich enough to press into a stranger's hand.

terms.explain: US novelist and Nashville bookstore owner. Bel Canto and The Dutch House made her famous. Whistler is the new one.
The national bestseller list from US independent bookstores, not Amazon.
A monthly list of books US indie booksellers swear you should read.

stories.image_alt: Hardcover of Ann Patchett's novel Whistler

stories.headline: Kathryn Stockett's Calamity Club parks at No. 3, 15 weeks in
stories.dek: The Help author's first novel in 17 years. 1930s Oxford, Mississippi. Spiegel & Grau. 35 dollars.
stories.caveman: Kathryn Stockett wrote The Help, which sold more than 15 million copies and became a movie. She went quiet for years. The Calamity Club, out May 5, is her return: 656 pages, Oxford, Mississippi, 1933. Three women — Meg, an 11-year-old nobody will adopt; Birdie, the loud unmarried sister; Charlie, a woman with a past — cook up a dangerous plan to take back their lives. US indies have it at No. 3 for the week ending Aug. 19, 15 weeks on the list. It was a May Indie Next pick. Stockett is from Jackson. She worked magazines in New York, then wrote the hit that made white-savior fights as loud as the book itself. This one again puts underestimated women in a Jim Crow town and asks what trouble they are allowed. Booksellers are still moving it in August, which is the real test, not pub week.
stories.why_it_matters: A 17-year gap, a 35-dollar hardcover, and still No. 3 on indies means Stockett's name still prints money — and still drags the old arguments about who gets to tell Mississippi.
stories.camps: Fans missed her big-hearted plots. Skeptics never forgave The Help. Booksellers will sell any novel that makes reading groups fight and then reorder.

terms.explain: US novelist from Jackson, Mississippi. The Help (2009) sold over 15 million copies. The Calamity Club is her long-awaited follow-up.
An independent-minded US publisher. It put out The Calamity Club at 35 dollars.
Monthly pick list from US independent booksellers.

stories.image_alt: The Calamity Club by Kathryn Stockett book cover

stories.headline: US book workers call this a hot labor summer after Hachette's giant union win
stories.dek: Publishers Weekly's Aug. 24 issue: about 600 Hachette staff joined the NewsGuild, the biggest trade-publishing union yet.
stories.caveman: For 80 years HarperCollins was the only Big Five house with a real union. That club got bigger. About 600 Hachette Book Group workers joined the Washington-Baltimore NewsGuild, the largest trade-publishing union in US history. Catapult workers, University of Chicago Press, and Dark Horse Comics also unionized or got recognized this year. PW's Aug. 24 magazine, circulating now, calls it a hot labor summer. Workers name the same rot: low pay, fat workloads, and a 'passion tax' — the idea that you should eat peanuts because you love books. Many say bosses clawed back work-from-home after COVID. HarperCollins already struck for three months in 2022-23. After that, other houses quietly lifted starting pay. Penguin Random House recently went from 51,000 to 55,000 dollars. Organizers want that in a contract, plus rules so AI cannot eat jobs. Hachette's CEO David Shelley said he will work with the union. The company had posted anti-union flyers first.
stories.why_it_matters: The people who make American books are mostly in New York, underpaid, and done pretending love is a benefit. Their fight sets the floor for what a 25-year-old editor can survive on.
stories.camps: Workers say a handshake benefit is not a right. Houses say they already raised pay. The NewsGuild wants AI clauses in writing. Younger staff, drowning in rent, are the engine.

terms.explain: One of the US Big Five publishers. Imprints include Little, Brown. About 600 staff just unionized.
A union that now represents Hachette staff as well as many journalists.
Worker slang for taking low pay because you love the work. Book people have paid it for decades.

stories.image_alt: Book publishing office or union action in US publishing

stories.headline: Colleen Hoover's Verity surges again as the Hathaway-Johnson trailer sells paper
stories.dek: PW's Aug. 24 bestseller notes: back to No. 4 trade paperback, more than 2.5 times last week's print sales. Film opens Oct. 2.
stories.caveman: Colleen Hoover is the US writer who turned online word-of-mouth into a machine. Verity, her nasty little thriller about a ghostwriter in a broken novelist's house, first came out in 2018. A movie trailer dropped Aug. 11. Anne Hathaway plays Verity. Dakota Johnson plays the hired writer. Josh Hartnett plays the husband. Amazon MGM opens the film Oct. 2. PW's weekly recap, out with the Aug. 24 issue, says the book jumped back to No. 4 on trade paperback with its fattest print week yet, more than two and a half times the week before. A movie-tie-in edition hit Aug. 18. This is the Hoover loop: screen heat, then stacks by the register. It is not new art. It is the market showing, again, that a trailer can still move paper in a country that supposedly quit reading.
stories.why_it_matters: When one 2018 thriller can triple its print week off a trailer, Hollywood is still the loudest US bookseller — louder than any indie staff pick.
stories.camps: Hoover readers want the movie to be messy. Snobs roll their eyes. Bookstores will take the units. Amazon made the film and also sells the book. That circle is the point.

terms.explain: US novelist. It Ends With Us and Verity turned BookTok fame into huge sales. Verity is now a movie.
The larger, nicer paperback format US stores put on front tables, not the small airport paperback.
A book reprint with the film's actors on the cover, timed to the trailer or the opening.

stories.image_alt: Verity book or Anne Hathaway and Dakota Johnson movie still

stories.headline: Somalia shuts 205 clinics as aid cuts send hungry children up 32 percent
stories.dek: UNICEF Friday from Nairobi: 1.9 million children may be malnourished this year. Water in the bush went from 2 dollars to 8.
stories.caveman: Somalia is dry, at war, and going broke on help. UNICEF's James Elder told Geneva on Friday, from Nairobi, that 205 health and nutrition posts already closed after rich countries slashed aid. Worst-case, 618 could shut. In the first half of 2026, children admitted with severe wasting and extra sickness rose 32 percent. Not because more kids got sick at once. Because the village clinic is gone, so they arrive later and sicker. About 1.9 million Somali children may go hungry this year. Almost 500,000 of them could be the deadly kind of thin. Drought killed herds. About 500,000 people fled between January and April. Rural water that cost 2 dollars a barrel now costs 8. The Iran war made fuel and fertilizer dearer. A fat El Niño may dump floods next. The US left Somalia out of a 2 billion dollar aid pledge, citing theft. Elder said the programs work. The money walked away.
stories.why_it_matters: Closing a feeding post is not a budget line. It is a mother walking farther with a baby who may not make it. This is what 'aid cuts' look like in a child's body.
stories.camps: UNICEF begs donors not to retreat at the worst time. Western capitals say they are tired and that Somalia leaks aid. Families in camps got clothes from poorer neighbors, not from the world.

terms.explain: The worst hunger in children. The body eats itself. Without fast treatment, many die.

stories.headline: Myanmar junta bombs a monastery; 14 people on a Buddhist retreat die
stories.dek: Friday morning, Myaung township, Sagaing. 11 men, 3 women. Locals told AFP.
stories.caveman: Myanmar's army dropped a bomb on a monastery hall at about 9 in the morning Friday. The people inside were on a meditation retreat for Buddhist Lent. Fourteen died: 11 men, 3 women. Five were from the village. Nine had come from nearby. The place is Myaung township in Sagaing, a dry-zone region that has fought the junta since the 2021 coup. Two local resistance fighters who helped pull bodies told AFP. The army did not put out a real account. This is how the war is fought now: from the air, against rooms full of civilians, because the junta does not hold the roads. Sagaing has seen this movie. Each strike adds to a pile of burned towns and empty schools. The country is a humanitarian wreck, and the people with the planes keep hitting places of prayer.
stories.why_it_matters: A monastery is not a barracks. If the junta can bomb a retreat and shrug, no civilian roof in the dry zone is safe, and aid workers cannot plan around that.
stories.camps: Resistance groups call it a war crime. The junta calls almost everyone a terrorist and says little. Neighbors in ASEAN still prefer quiet. The dead cannot vote in the junta's planned poll.

terms.explain: The generals who seized Myanmar in 2021 and still rule by force and air strikes.
A region in central Myanmar. Much of it is in revolt. The monastery was in Myaung township.
The monsoon retreat months when many Buddhists stay at monasteries to meditate.

stories.headline: UN probe: South Sudan is close to new atrocity crimes as a shaky vote nears
stories.dek: Thursday commission report, still echoing into the weekend. First national elections since independence, almost no guardrails.
stories.caveman: South Sudan got independence in 2011, then ate itself in a civil war. A UN human-rights commission said Thursday the country is again near the cliff. It listed warning signs for genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes, and ethnic cleansing, and said most of those signs are flashing at once. A national election is being rushed, the first since independence, without a real ceasefire watch, independent courts, or an open political field. Commissioners named impunity, corrupt exclusive rule, shrinking civic space, and hate talk. The tools that might slow a slide — monitors, justice, talks — are weak or off. 'Fifteen years after independence, South Sudan is at one of its most dangerous points,' they wrote. The window to stop a rerun of 2013-2018 killing and flight is closing, they said, but not shut. The crisis is under-reported. That is part of the danger.
stories.why_it_matters: When a UN atrocity panel says the window is closing, it is telling donors and neighbors: a bad election here will not be a local mess. It will be graves and refugees.
stories.camps: The commission wants the vote slowed until safeguards exist. Juba's elite wants an election that locks in power. Civilians remember the last war and have nowhere cheap to run.

terms.explain: The worst international crimes: genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes, ethnic cleansing.

terms.explain: An independent UN probe that reports on abuses and warning signs in South Sudan.

stories.headline: Guinea-Bissau's first mpox outbreak: half the suspected cases are children
stories.dek: UNICEF: 23 of 46 suspected cases are under 15. Sixteen are toddlers. Schools reopen in September.
stories.caveman: Tiny West African state Guinea-Bissau had never recorded mpox. Then it declared an outbreak on July 4. UN News on Thursday, still the live alert, said 46 people are suspected. Twenty-three are children under 15. Sixteen of those are under four. Only seven cases are lab-confirmed, all adults, no deaths yet. Confirmed spots: six in Bissau city, one in Biombo. UNICEF's Sandra Martins called even a small first outbreak a big public-health event because the watch system is weak. Cases may be hiding. Health teams cannot yet see how the virus jumps. Mpox often stays mild in healthy adults. Babies get it worse. Schools open in September, which is a mixing bowl. UNICEF wants just over 150,000 dollars for tracing, tests, clean water in clinics, and honest messages so families are not shamed out of care. That is pocket change next to a bomber. It is not arriving fast.
stories.why_it_matters: First outbreaks in weak health systems are how a containable virus becomes a children's ward problem. A 150,000-dollar gap should not be a cliff.
stories.camps: UNICEF wants flexible cash now. The government says it is on it. Neighbors watch the border. Stigma is already a risk: if parents hide a rash, tracing dies.

terms.explain: A virus that causes rash, fever, and swollen nodes. Usually mild. Very young children can get much sicker.
A small West African country. This is its first known mpox outbreak.
